title_tag: Group Coaching Program: How to Build One | Mike Moll
meta_description: Dusty Jenkins thought he needed a full curriculum to launch his dads group. How to build a group coaching program, price it per call and write its page.
h1: How to create a group coaching program
sub: Dusty Jenkins wanted to launch a group for dads through Valiant Voyages, but he felt he needed a full program built first. On this live coaching episode we worked out a simpler offer: an open monthly membership, a price that reads per call, a landing page that leads with the outcome, and the confidence to charge for it.

guest.name: Dusty Jenkins
guest.bio: Dusty founded Valiant Voyages for fathers who feel distracted and want to be more intentional with their families, with themselves and at work. He also helps retreat hosts capture what happens at their retreats, and video production is his specialty.

short_answer.q: How do you create a group coaching program people will pay for?
short_answer.a: Sell support and access before you build a curriculum. People join a group to stay accountable and to be around others who get them. Set one monthly price with no end date, run group calls with breakout rooms, and let members stay as long as they like. Talk to early buyers first, then write the page from their words.

takeaways: People join a coaching group for access, accountability and support, so you can launch before the curriculum is done.
An open monthly membership lets you run the group with a big crowd without kicking anyone out when a program ends.
I showed Dusty that two calls on a $150 monthly plan come to $75 each, which is cheaper than therapy.
Lead the landing page with the outcome, and put a sub headline, proof and a call to action above the fold.
In the early days, make the call to action a call with you, and write the page from what buyers tell you.
Ask yourself if you'd buy the group. If you would, people like you will too, and the offer doesn't need a pile of extras.

sections.h2: What makes people pay for a group coaching program?
sections.html:
People pay for access, support and a group that holds them to their word. Dusty Jenkins came on the show feeling stuck. He didn't have a six-week coaching program fully built for his dads group, Valiant Voyages. The curriculum matters far less than he thought. I have clients who pay me thousands of dollars a month because they like the accountability of talking to me. They also like that I often have a fix for their problem that they haven't thought of yet.

I compared it to joining a baseball team. A team makes you exercise and it makes you see people. On a team, you go to the gym because you can't let the others down. People join a coaching group for the same reason: to hold themselves to something and to have people around who support them.

Dusty wants to reach fathers who feel distracted and want to be more intentional with their families. The founder of a company I work with that runs addiction recovery intensives told me community is one of the biggest parts of recovery. I think dads need that kind of place too, because most of them won't talk about this stuff with their co-workers.

sections.h2: How should you structure a group coaching program?
sections.html:
Set it up as an open membership with a monthly price, and let people stay for as long as they want support. I told Dusty I wouldn't build it as a six-week or one-year course with a set curriculum. Let the group grow into what its members need. You could have a hundred dads in one group, with a share each week, a group exercise and breakout rooms. That works with a big group, and you never have to kick anyone out when a program ends.

I took the format from a men's group I was in for a few months. Everyone got five minutes to share. When the group got too big, the host split us into breakout rooms of up to four people. Each person had three minutes for something going well and three minutes for something they were stuck on. At the end, you got three minutes of feedback from the others in your circle. I found those small, timed rooms amazing because they worked like little masterminds, and you met different people with different ideas.

The host picked a topic each week, and there was an accountability piece too. You set a goal for the month, like going to the gym three days a week. If you missed it, you owed 200 burpees and had to send the video.

sections.h2: How much should you charge for group coaching?
sections.html:
For Dusty's group, I suggested something like $150 a month, for as long as a member wants support. Break the price down per call, and it looks small next to what members get. I pointed out to Dusty that $150 a month for two calls comes to $75 a call. I told him that is cheaper than therapy, and probably better than therapy.

Most of the guys I went to high school with are married with two kids. They will never spend four hours a week on therapy work like I do. Picture one call on a Wednesday night from 7:00 to 8:30, in a safe place to unload and get advice. I told Dusty that for $75 a call, that's nothing.

Dusty shared his own example: he is in a coaching program with two 90-minute sessions a month, one where the coach teaches and one for open questions. The men's group I was in cost me $80 a month for one call every other Sunday and a WhatsApp group. If it had been run better, with the type of people I wanted to be around, I said I probably would have paid more.

sections.h2: Should a group coaching program start online or in person?
sections.html:
Start online, and add in-person meetups once members ask for them. Dusty's first plan was local pop-up dinner workshops and overnight trips for dads. He already travels to retreats for work, and he said each trip means about five days away from his family. Dusty saw that running dinners once or twice a month wouldn't pay the bills if this was his full-time work.

A one-day event in one city is hard to sell when your audience is small. When you host an online group, members start to ask if they can meet up. Say you have 87 dads spread across the US. You can plan a retreat in Atlanta for the ones who want to come.

Dusty took the idea further. In his plan, a local dinner with eight seats becomes a perk of the membership. He can pop up wherever members are, like a Colorado crew in June. I added that he can see where people sign up from and hold the meetup in the middle.

Finding your first membersDo your buyers spend time in Facebook groups? My episode with Megan Van Noy covers how to market a coaching offer there.

sections.h2: What should a coaching landing page say above the fold?
sections.html:
Above the fold, a visitor should see four things: a headline with the outcome, a sub headline that tells them they're in the right place, a call to action, and proof. Dusty's page had one of the four. His headline asked dads if they felt like a distracted father, then said "Let's be intentional together." I would lead with the outcome the dad wants. Something like "We help fathers become more intentional," with a sub headline about turning distracted, distant dads into the men they want to be.

Opening on the negative pushes on a dad who may already feel low about himself as a father. Many coaches lead with the pain. I told Dusty that this is my own opinion, and that I've been moving toward leading with the dream.

For proof, a one-sentence testimonial works, or a line like "over 20 five-star reviews on Google." Then add a button with the next step.

sections.h2: What goes below the fold on a coaching landing page?
sections.html:
Right below the fold, describe the product and how members get the outcome. For Dusty, that means saying plainly that this is an online support group where Christian dads come together. Put the proof and the program first, and save your own story for further down. I told Dusty to move everything about himself into one section near the end, with a "Hi, I'm Dusty" heading. That includes the story about his nine-year-old daughter.

Before the program, describe the challenge dads share. They're busy, they have less time to see friends, and they have no one to lean on. Then show what the program is and what members get from it.

When you write those benefits, start with what the member gets and follow with how it happens. I gave Dusty an example. For "two group coaching calls every month," write "feel supported by other dads in our bi-weekly group calls." For "WhatsApp group," write "stay in touch and build community through our group WhatsApp." For the third, write: get a fresh set of eyes and ears on the challenges you face as a parent, from dads like you.

sections.h2: What should your call to action be when you're starting out?
sections.html:
Early on, make the call to action a call with you, and get on the phone with as many people as you can. Dusty asked whether it should be a 15-minute call or a form to see if the group is right for them. Those first calls are your customer research. You don't know yet what makes someone want a group like this.

Ask them to tell you about themselves and why they think a group like this would help. Ask what they'd most want to take away, and what would be a win if they joined.

Use what they tell you as the words on the landing page. For Dusty, the headline and the benefits would come from what dads told him they want. The rest of his page, like the "Dad, can you play?" story about pushing kids off, can stay below that.

sections.h2: How do you get the confidence to charge more for coaching?
sections.html:
Picture yourself as the buyer, and ask if you would pay for it. I know Dusty well, and he overthinks. Everyone on the planet has some impostor syndrome (the feeling of being a fraud), but he lets it steer his decisions. Dusty is his own customer, so if he would pay for the group, other dads like him will too. I asked him to imagine a group of supportive dads where he could share his wins and what he thinks he's screwing up. I think Dusty would pay $150 a month for two calls with them.

Dusty said his overthinking tells him to list every benefit so the money seems to stretch. I charge a lot more now, and I do fewer things for each client. I used to hand clients a list of 17 things we'd tackle together. Now I tell them that to fix the problem they care about, we go back to the root and fix three things. When they want that fixed, I tell them it's 15 grand. They say it sounds good, because the result will make them far more money than that.

For Dusty's group, I said the offer is the support of other dads and getting a little better as a father every month, for $150 a month.

Raising your priceHas your offer grown a long list of deliverables? How to raise your prices without adding more work covers which ones to cut as the price goes up.

sections.h2: What can you do this week?
sections.html:
1. Write down what you would want from your group if you were the buyer, and how much a month it would be worth to you.
  2. Set one monthly price with no end date, and work out what it comes to per call.
  3. Get on calls with as many people who might join as you can, and ask what a win would be for them.
  4. Change your headline to the outcome, and put a sub headline, proof and a button at the top of the page.
  5. Turn each feature on your page into a benefit, with the feature after it.

If you're not sure yet who the group is for, my episode with Susie Ippolito covers how to pick your ideal client.

paragraphs.text: All right, on this episode we have Dusty Jenkins from Valiant Voyages. Oh man, I'm really bad with stringing together names of people and the names of the company. I don't know why, it's like four words. Come on, Mike. Anyway, brother, thank you for coming on. Good to see you.

paragraphs.speaker: Dusty
paragraphs.text: Super pumped to be here. Thanks, Mike. I really appreciate your time today, and excited to see what we dive into.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: Yeah, man. So Dusty and I met for the first time... we've known each other on the internet for a while through a mutual friend, and this February, so geez, last month, that's crazy, in Playa del Carmen we met at a conference. I got to talking, and I think what he's building is really cool. So we're going to dive into positioning and product today. But why don't you give the audience, the people that are listening to you, the two-minute synopsis of what it is that you're building?

paragraphs.speaker: Dusty
paragraphs.text: Yeah, thanks, Mike. So it's been kind of a dream that came about in 2020. I went through some struggles in my marriage, where I almost lost my marriage, and during that time, as I was seeking help through some addictions that I was facing, I got this dream to reach out to other men that were going through the same thing that I was. And I used a lot of fear and shame to not pursue that dream for a really long time. I mean, not a long time, but three years, roughly.

paragraphs.speaker: Dusty
paragraphs.text: And just recently, diving into other coaching programs and that kind of thing, getting some of that positive reinforcement, I guess, on like, hey, maybe this is an issue that needs to be talked about more. And so I just took a step of faith and decided I'm going to launch this thing. And so Valiant Voyages came about, and it's directed towards fathers who feel distracted in life and simply want to be more intentional with their families, with themselves, and themselves in the workplace as well. So that's the gist of it.

paragraphs.speaker: Dusty
paragraphs.text: It's basically paired with an experience in nature and spirituality. My foundation is with Jesus Christ, and so there is that element. However, it's not a judgmental thing. A lot of people get hung up on this religion versus relationship, and I'm on the relationship side of it. So I never come at anybody with judgment or anything like that. We're all making the same mistakes, just in different ways.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: Got it. And so obviously dads is the target market. Are you only focused on people locally, or are you thinking about an online piece of this?

paragraphs.speaker: Dusty
paragraphs.text: Yeah, so locally for sure. But the unique thing about this is, as a father traveling to other retreats, and that's what I do professionally, I help retreat hosts capture the magic that happens, I find myself burning two days in travel getting there and home, then the two-and-a-half-day experience. So it's about five days away from the family.

paragraphs.speaker: Dusty
paragraphs.text: And as I was dreaming about bringing something to life for dads, I was thinking, man, the families at home are already typically not seeing Dad too much, and so to pull him out of that environment even more just felt not great. So I thought, well, maybe I'll start locally and just do these little pop-up dinner type workshops, overnight experiences. That's a low impact on their schedule and time, but we get to pour in a lot of love in that amount of time.

paragraphs.speaker: Dusty
paragraphs.text: And so my goal is, I have opportunities all over the nation, really, and down into the Dominican Republic, but to kind of pop these up and focus the marketing on the local demographic for that area. So less people flying into them, and just sending maybe a geo-targeted ad or something like that to the dads in that area.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: Got it. And have you thought at all about... because one thing, I've been working with this company that does sex addiction intensives. So there's these four-day things where it's like, if you're trying to save your marriage, and things are going very sideways, and you've relapsed with your sex addiction, come to this thing. And it's a very thought-through, very planned experience.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: But one of the things, I've spoken with the founder of that, and he's a million-dollar-a-year coach as well, and what he said, and what his mastermind group said, is that one of the biggest things with addiction recovery is community. And not that being an absent or not a connected dad is in that realm, but I do wonder if you should have an online group community piece of this that exists.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: Because I look at it from the business lens, where I'm part of a few different business communities. I work solo, I work from wherever I am in the world, I've been on a computer for 10 years, and sometimes it's nice to just bounce ideas off of somebody, or have the support of, hey, can someone look at this thing for me, or, hey, I'm struggling with this thing, what's going on? And I think people nowadays, more than ever since COVID, have been more isolated, and a lot of people haven't gone back to the same level of socialization as before. And I just wonder if having that avenue in your business might be beneficial, maybe over time.

paragraphs.speaker: Dusty
paragraphs.text: Yeah, I think that's definitely where I could see it going in the very near future, because trying to do these once or twice a month is not going to be sustainable financially if this is going to be my full-time thing. So yeah, I do love the idea of an online community, where we can keep weekly check-ins, challenges, that kind of thing, and just talk about what's coming up for these guys week to week.

paragraphs.speaker: Dusty
paragraphs.text: So I think that's a little bit where I'm stuck, having that impostor syndrome, right? Not having the coaching program fully fleshed out. Like, what could a six-week program look like, or even longer, to guide them through step by step? That's kind of something to think about.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: Here's the truth about coaching. The program doesn't matter at all. I have people that pay me thousands of dollars a month because they like the accountability of being able to talk to me. They like that when we get on a call, I probably have a solution to their problem that they haven't thought about yet. And we've achieved the financial goals, the programming is done, but people want support. People want access. And so the way that you're thinking about it, as a curriculum, I don't think people give a [bleep]. I think people are very willing to pay for access to the place that makes them feel comfortable.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: Think about it like this. Think about it like a sports league, right? I join a baseball team. Why do I join a baseball team? It forces me to exercise, it forces me to socialize, and unlike me going to the gym by myself, I'm like, well, I can't let the team down. We're not going to let Gary play second base, that's a disaster. I better go, right? And so we join these things to make ourselves accountable, to make ourselves obligated to a thing, to have the community, to have that support.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: So I don't think the programming matters. If I were you, I wouldn't structure it in a year, or in six weeks, this is the curriculum you're going to learn. I would just let it blossom into a thing. You could have a hundred dads in a thing where each week you come in to share something, or you do some group exercise, and you have your breakout rooms, or you structure it like that, where you could do this at scale where you don't have to kick people out. It could just be like 100 bucks or 150 bucks a month for as long as you want to be supported by the community.

paragraphs.speaker: Dusty
paragraphs.text: Yeah, oh, I like that. That's a lot more simplified than getting the private chef and the venue and the whole thing. It's like, man, that took a lot of energy. And it's like, oh, putting together an online community and getting to have some awesome conversations, like this even, is just as impactful sometimes.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: Well, and I think what happens is, as that builds, and as you are the host of this virtual party, this virtual support, what ends up happening is they say, so can we meet up sometime?

paragraphs.speaker: Dusty
paragraphs.text: Yeah, that could be.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: And then all of a sudden you're like, okay, I've got this group of like 87 dads scattered across the US. Hey, we're going to do this retreat in Atlanta, or in this countryside place. Then you do it. Because I think trying to sell tickets to a one-day thing, where it's stuck on a specific day in a specific geo, when your audience is very small, probably makes it way more difficult than if you already have an audience and they're already thirsting for more, like, I would love to come and meet you guys.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: I was in this group for a period of time. It was kind of a group for men. I only stayed in it for a few months, just because I was looking for more entrepreneurial-focused people, so that group wasn't the group. But it was called something like We Are Men, and it was great. Everybody had five minutes to share some piece, right?

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: And if the group got too big, we would put it into breakout rooms with up to four people, and it was like, okay, everybody share something that's gone really well, you've got three minutes, and then something that you're struggling with, you have three minutes. And then at the end, you have three minutes for the other members in your circle to give you feedback or some thoughts on how to solve that issue.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: And those little breakout room masterminds were amazing, because we could talk within our little pods of people, and you would connect with different people, so you'd have different ideas, and everything is timed, almost like a mastermind. I found that to be very impactful. And it was not a program-length thing. The owner came up with a thing, and he goes, hey, this week we're going to talk about whatever.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: And then we would also do accountability things. So, what's your exercising thing for this month? And it was like, okay, I'm going to go to the gym three days a week. So there was an accountability piece once a week, and then if you failed your thing, you owed 200 burpees and you had to send the video. You know what I mean?

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: So it was these community-oriented conversations, and things of, how do we make ourselves better as a group of men. And I feel like that could be really powerful, because I think dads typically don't have that place to go. Okay, we might have the sports leagues, but you're not going to talk to your co-workers about this stuff. And so where is that outlet? And I think you could be a great outlet for that.

paragraphs.speaker: Dusty
paragraphs.text: Dude, I love that. It's all super helpful for sure. I like how that feels as well. I think the thing that kind of came to my mind was, if there's that monthly membership, let's say it is the $100 a month, the monthly meetup, especially for the local dads, could just be a perk. It's like, hey, if you're available, we only have eight seats available, but your membership includes the opportunity to come and do this dinner workshop. And then I can just kind of have those little pop-ups based on memberships, like you said. Hey, here's my Colorado crew, I'm headed to Colorado in June.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: Yeah, and it could just be organic and small until you know where your people are coming from. And then you might see a trend of where people are signing up. Okay, well, we've got a bunch of people here and a bunch of people here, let's do the meetup in the middle. But I think that low time commitment, and then for you, the low overhead, where you're just being a facilitator.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: For this men's group, I was paying, I think, 90 bucks a month. No, 80 bucks a month. But to be honest, if it was better facilitated and it was the type of people I wanted to be around, I probably would have paid more. We had one call every two weeks, it was every other Sunday, and there was nothing in between. It was just that. And there was a WhatsApp group, and he would shoot some stuff out, hey, this is a cool thing to check out, and some people would spin off conversations.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: But I think about business consulting, and if I were to break it down by how much I charge per phone call, it's basically like a thousand dollars per phone call, right? And for a lot of people that doesn't make sense, because they're not business owners. But for someone who's like, oh, 75 bucks, if it's 150 a month, it's 75 bucks per phone call. It's cheaper than therapy. It's probably better than therapy. So there you go, there's your therapy, you know what I mean?

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: And you could potentially try and structure it in a way where they could write it off, if they have health insurance. Maybe get an accreditation or certification over time, or I don't know, maybe just position it in a way that they might be able to write it off. I would look at how I would structure this so they write it off as part of their therapy benefits through their company. I don't know if you'd be able to without being certified or a doctor, but something to play with.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: But if you break it down that way, you're like, well, 150 bucks a month, but if it's two calls, and I come on the call and I leave feeling like I got those things out, because where's the outlet otherwise, right? Where is the outlet for men? We don't have it. Maybe it's talk therapy. For me, I've been working like crazy. paragraphs.text: I think about most of the guys that I know, and all of my friends from high school are married with two kids, they have their house, they have their whatever. For 75 bucks a call, that's nothing.

paragraphs.speaker: Dusty
paragraphs.text: Yeah, that's good. I'm in a program right now. It's like 300 a month, and it's two 90-minute sessions a month, basically. paragraphs.speaker: Dusty
paragraphs.text: What are your thoughts on the Valiant Voyages landing page, as far as the structure goes? I feel like I need more. paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: Yeah, perfect. So what I'll do is share it on the screen for anybody watching on YouTube, but for any of the podcast listeners, I will describe the pieces of it and break that down.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: So the headline is, "Feeling like a distracted father? Let's be intentional together." I don't love that, because it's starting with a negative. You almost want to lead with the outcome first. Like, we help fathers become more intentional, right? paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: And then you can say underneath, we help distracted dads get in tune with their family and become a better father, or something like that. The sub headline could be that, right? But where we're landing here, the first conversation thread is, do I feel like a distracted father? You're almost pushing at that negative. You're almost pushing at, yeah, I know I'm not a great dad. Okay. That's the first thing I read.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: Now, there is one thing that says pain sells. So this is a very subjective opinion of mine, but I've been moving in the direction of leading more with candy, which is, let's lead towards the dream. Become a more intentional father, or we help you become a more intentional father. And then the sub headline could be turning distracted and distant dads into the man that they want to be, or something like that. To me, that's kind of a nice thing.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: And then the next section, which is that little conversation thing, "Dad, can you play?" "In a minute, let me finish..." I think what you might want to put ahead of that is a little bit more reinforcement that the person's in the right place.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: So what you want to do is, above the fold, you want to have four main things, and right now you've got kind of one of the four. Right now you've got the headline, the logo, and then just the text, "Dad, can you play?" And so what you want to have in the front is a reinforcement of, am I the right person, am I in the right place?

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: So, is this me, number one, and is this the thing that I need, number two. We need a call to action, so we need a button, or some, this is the next step, on this first page before we scroll, before we touch anything. And then we also need credibility. So whether that's over 20 five-star reviews on Google, or just a small one-sentence testimonial from somebody.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: Because internet scrollers, all of us, we don't realize how distracted we are and how distracted we get, and we don't realize that we need to be told what to do, and it needs to happen very quickly. So every landing page should have the headline, so the outcome, or a description of the outcome that you provide, so they're like, oh, I want that. A sub headline that says, oh, I am that person. And then the testimonial, which is, oh, someone else has trusted this guy to do this thing. Cool, what do I do next? And so we should have a call to action there. So that's how I would change this top part.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: And then typically, the next section is, okay, I've identified that I want the thing, I've identified that I'm in the category of the people, and then there's a call to action. But I might not be sold yet, because, okay, I want the thing, but what do I need to do to get the thing? So we need to describe the product a little bit. So how we get there, or what this thing is, should come next.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: So if it's the group thing, an online dad support group where Christian dads come together, and if you want to do the religion thing or not, doesn't matter, but that should be the next thing. So now I can identify: I want it, I'm that guy, someone else trusted this guy. The next step is, what do I need to do to get there? So we need to start talking about our process, or the steps, or what is the product.

paragraphs.speaker: Dusty
paragraphs.text: And are we still talking about above the fold?

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: No, that could be just below.

paragraphs.speaker: Dusty
paragraphs.text: Okay, cool. So going back to above the fold, the call to action, would you recommend that being like a 15-minute call, or a form, fill out this form to see if this group is right for you? What would be your idea on the call to action there?

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: In the early stages, what you want to do is probably get on the call with as many people as possible to help validate what it is that they're looking for. So if you're going to be intentional about that call, try and find out, hey, tell me about you, tell me about why you think a group like this would be beneficial.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: What's the number one takeaway that you would want? What would be a win if you joined this group? Because you don't know exactly what the motivation of the person is. So you're getting consumer research done on that phone call, especially for the first bit. And then when you know that information, that becomes the landing page, and then the landing page can sell itself.

paragraphs.speaker: Dusty
paragraphs.text: Cool, that's super helpful.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: Yeah, and then you can go into this other stuff, like, does this resonate with you? "Dad, can I play?" Pushing off your kids, ignoring them. So all the rest of it is decent.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: What I would do is put everything about you into one section, because right now it kind of says, my nine-year-old daughter, like it's a story, and then it's kind of an about me. Tell that all in one section and move it a little bit down. I would move it like: this is what the programming is, this is why we do it the way we do, this is what other people say about it, and then a "Hi, I'm Dusty." That's the best way.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: So structurally, it should go: the header, which is social proof, am I in the right place, what should I do next. And then it's the extra bit of validation, so the next part is reaffirming that they're in the right place. And then either your story, or, our dads have this experience. So what is the challenge?

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: We're busy, we have less time to go out and socialize and be with friends, and as a result of that, the isolation and not having any support creates friction, point A and C, and so we created, boom. And then it's, what is the program? So benefit, benefit, benefit, what's in it, or what they're going to get with this thing. And then talk about you.

paragraphs.speaker: Dusty
paragraphs.text: Cool.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: Yeah, and the key with the benefits is, don't write the features. Don't write, two group coaching calls every month, WhatsApp group with whatever. Those are the functions. Get a fresh set of eyes and ears on challenges that you're facing in parenthood from other dads just like you. Stay in touch and build community through our Discord channel, or our group WhatsApp, or whatever the case may be. So start with, what am I getting from this, what's the benefit, and then the function of how it's going to happen.

paragraphs.speaker: Dusty
paragraphs.text: Dude, I love it, man. This is all super helpful. I knew it would be awesome, man.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: Well, we covered a lot there. And I just think, for you, knowing you personally, you're an overthinker, and you have a lot of ongoing impostor syndrome. It's not just you, it's literally everybody on the planet. But I think with you, you let it seep into you, and you let it narrate some of your decision-making. And I think the truth is, think about what you would buy for you, and build that thing.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: And so if you took an honest step back and said, hey, if there was a group of dads that were really chill and supportive, and I got to talk to them and share my wins as a father, my challenges, the things that I think I'm screwing up, and get some feedback, would I pay 150 bucks a month to jump on two calls with these people? paragraphs.speaker: Dusty
paragraphs.text: Cool, yeah, that's helpful. paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: And here's the truth. My coaching product has gotten significantly more expensive with significantly less deliverables. paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: I just have, if we're going to solve this problem, we need to go back to the root and fix A, B and C so that D works out. Very good, do you want to fix D? People are like, yeah. paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: But my old habit was being like, oh, if I just add more stuff, then the perceived value is going to be higher. But I don't want more stuff. I just want an outcome. So that's worth that money for them.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: And so I think it's just, hey, if you had the support of other dads, and you could enter every single month being just a little bit better of a father, would you pay 150 bucks a month for that? It doesn't need anything else. It is the thing.

paragraphs.text: Yeah, yeah, that's so good. Simplify. I like simple.
